summary:
TIERRA is an interactive web map that finds and explains places on Earth that resemble the surface of Mars or the Moon. It goes beyond listing well-known analog sites by researching overlooked regions as well.

The platform centers on one satellite map of Earth. Small markers distinguish established analog sites from newly investigated candidates. Clicking a marker opens a simple panel with the site’s coordinates, local environment, the matching Mars or Moon region, side-by-side comparisons, and links to supporting research and NASA data.

The design is minimal and slightly vintage: dark, muted colors, small markers, and no clutter or heavy animation. It’s built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet.js, using satellite imagery, NASA datasets, and peer-reviewed research. The goal is to use visual exploration to identify and scientifically validate new terrestrial analogs.

Even shorter version: TIERRA is a satellite map of Earth that highlights known and newly proposed sites resembling Mars and the Moon. Each marker opens a data panel with coordinates, environmental details, planetary comparisons, and NASA and research references, all in a clean, minimal interface.
details:
TIERRA (Terrestrial Analog Explorer) is an interactive web map that presents places on Earth whose geology and environment resemble those of Mars and the Moon. It shows both identified analogs and newly proposed candidates. Each site appears as a marker on a satellite map of Earth, and clicking a marker opens a small window with the site’s details: coordinates, environmental characteristics, its Mars or Moon counterpart, and supporting research. Users can search by country or site name, filter by planetary target, classification, and analog characteristics, and add their own placemarks. A side panel summarizes the research inventory, which currently covers 42 sites.

The platform gathers scattered analog research into one visual, searchable tool. This helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts compare terrestrial and planetary environments quickly. Its intended impact is to make comparative planetology more accessible, to encourage research on overlooked regions of Earth, and to support future mission planning, astronaut training, and technology testing in places that are cheaper and easier to reach than other worlds.

TIERRA was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Leaflet.js for the interactive mapping and Esri satellite imagery as the base layer. Its content draws on NASA datasets and peer-reviewed planetary research, and it runs in any web browser with no special hardware.

The project is creative in treating the map as a research tool rather than a static list: it separates “found” from “possible” analogs, and it lets users contribute new locations. Its minimal, slightly vintage scientific-interface style keeps the focus on the data. The team considered scientific accuracy, clear and uncluttered design, ease of use, accessibility on a lightweight web stack, and the ability to grow as new analogs are discovered.
